title: Going back to first principles, on purpose
excerpt: Six years shipping production agentic systems taught me how to build with LLMs. Now I'm going back through the fundamentals properly, in the open.
body:
## Why write in the open

Most of my technical growth over the last few years has come from shipping - multi-agent platforms, retrieval pipelines, fine-tuned classifiers running in production. That's real experience, but it's a specific kind: applied engineering optimises for *what works in production*, which isn't always the same muscle as understanding *why* something works from first principles.

I got properly interested in this during a university AI module that went from the fundamentals through CNNs and transformers - that's what pulled me toward this field in the first place. Since then, the applied side has moved fast, and I want to go back through the fundamentals deliberately: not because I'm starting from zero, but because the gap between "I studied this" and "I could rebuild it and explain every decision" is worth closing properly, especially with how quickly the field's moved on since.

This is the first post in a series doing exactly that - working back through the fundamentals (attention from scratch, policy gradient methods, reward modelling) and writing up what I learn, including the parts I get wrong the first time.

### What's next

- A transformer implemented from scratch, no framework shortcuts
- Notes on PPO vs DPO for preference optimisation
- Reward modelling experiments on small open datasets

If you're doing something similar - refreshing and deepening fundamentals alongside applied work - I'd like to hear what worked for you.

title: Using contextual bandits to make RAG systems adaptive
excerpt: Exploring how reinforcement learning techniques can help retrieval systems adapt as query patterns change - and the challenges that come with feedback-driven optimisation.
body:
## The problem

Static RAG configurations can degrade as query patterns change over time. Retrieval strategies that work well for one group of queries may become less effective as requirements evolve, making continuous evaluation and adaptation important.

One approach I have been exploring is using contextual bandits to help systems select between different retrieval and generation strategies based on feedback signals. By using time-weighted rewards, newer observations can have more influence than older ones when measuring performance.

### Challenges with feedback-driven optimisation

- **Reward attribution lag.** Feedback often arrives after an interaction, making it challenging to correctly associate outcomes with the actions that produced them.
- **Cold-start variance.** New strategies require exploration before enough signal exists to understand their effectiveness.
- **Reward model drift.** When evaluation relies on models such as LLM-based judges, the evaluation process itself needs monitoring to ensure optimisation targets the right behaviours.

Adaptive AI systems introduce interesting optimisation challenges and provide opportunities for building more robust retrieval pipelines.

title: Reading the scan or reading the report? A Kaggle bronze and what 58 expert-labelled knee MRIs show
excerpt: My bronze medal in the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) Knee Abnormality Detection challenge, and how, on 58 expert-labelled studies, artificial intelligence (AI) models trained on report-derived labels ranked findings that the report left out lower than findings it mentioned.
body: Many of the big public medical imaging datasets weren't labelled by someone looking at every scan, because that's slow and expensive. Instead, the labels were pulled out of the radiology report: if the report says "anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear", the scan gets an ACL-tear label. That raises a question I kept coming back to during this competition: **is the artificial intelligence (AI) learning what's on the scan, or what the radiologist chose to write down?** Those aren't the same thing: radiologists write for a referring doctor and may leave out things they consider minor. ## The competition and the result The challenge, run on Kaggle by the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), asked for models that spot 12 abnormalities on knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans (ligament tears, meniscus tears, arthritis, fluid in the joint, synovitis, Baker's cyst, bone bruising and fracture). It was scored with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), a score that measures how well a model ranks the cases that have a problem above the ones that don't (1.0 is perfect; 0.5 is guessing). I finished with a **bronze medal, 506th of 6,425 teams (top 8%)**, with a private score of 0.943. On the public leaderboard I'd been 799th, so I moved up 293 places when the final scores were revealed. (Kaggle still has to verify the results, so the standings are provisional for now.) I want to be upfront about credit. The models in my medal submission weren't mine. They came from public notebooks shared by the community, mainly **goodpjw2008's** public "v27" blend recipe and reader model, with leaderboard-tuned weights from **heliosli** and work from **nartaa**, **varshithakolupuri** and **rostigor**, plus report-label sets shared by other competitors (**riadmohamed42**, **stevenleehans**, **pilkwang**, **lixin73**, **xhaitanya** and **yunusgmsoy**), and the Raptor model lineage from **dreaddevelopment**. My own work was: - **Expert-label weighting of the blend**: moving v27's per-finding weights part of the way toward whichever models ranked the 58 expert-labelled studies best. - **The seen/silent/report-only comparison** described below. - **Robustness checks**: swapping left and right knee predictions, testing whether errors were linked to the number of MRI series, a random label-flip noise test, re-reading the reports that had first been read cut short, and retraining my own small model with the 58 expert studies held out. ## The key question: what do expert labels reveal? The training set had about 4,400 knee MRI studies. Almost all came with only a free-text report, which competitors had to turn into labels. But **58 studies came with per-finding labels supplied by the organisers**. The organisers thank a team of radiologists, recruited through two skeletal radiology societies, for labelling the challenge data, so I call these "expert labels": a direct yes/no for each finding, rather than whatever a report happened to mention. They aren't guaranteed to be right, though, because the labelling process isn't published. The hidden test set's labelling method isn't published either. My bet was that it's labelled more like those 58 studies than like the reports. So I took the public v27 blend and moved its per-finding weights part of the way toward whichever models ranked the expert labels best. On the private leaderboard, every expert-weighted blend I submitted scored 0.943, and every non-expert version of v27 scored 0.942. That's only +0.001, one unit at the precision Kaggle displays, with no confidence interval, so it's consistent with my bet but doesn't prove it. ## What happens when reports miss a finding? The 58 studies also let me test the bigger question. For each study and finding, I compared the expert label with whether the report mentioned it. That splits the expert-positive findings into two groups: - **Seen**: the expert says it's there, and the report mentions it. - **Silent**: the expert says it's there, but the report doesn't mention it. Across those 58 studies there were 199 seen findings and 41 silent ones. Then I checked how well each model ranked them against findings that were absent in both the expert label and the report. *Left: how well each model ranks reported (blue), silent (orange) and report-only (green) findings. Right: the gap between reported and silent findings, with 95% intervals that all sit above zero. Figure from my analysis; apart from my own small model, the models compared are the public notebooks credited above.* The pattern was the same for all eight models and blends I looked at, from the individual public models and their blends to a small model of my own: - **Reported findings** were ranked very well (AUC 0.96–0.98). - **Silent findings** were ranked lower (AUC 0.79–0.87). - That's a **gap of about 0.11–0.18 AUC**, and for every model the 95% confidence interval excluded zero. The direction was consistent across every model, though with only 58 studies the exact size is uncertain. The 95% intervals come from resampling whole studies (not individual findings) with replacement, 4,000 times, and recomputing each number every time. **Were the models just remembering these 58 studies?** I checked what each model's authors published. The R6 model's training manifest records zero of the 58 in training, and the reader model's published label script keeps them out of training. For the Raptor models it isn't documented. My own small model had trained on 47 of the 58, so I retrained it three times with all 58 left out (and three times with them left in, for comparison), then scored the 58 with the competition's inference code. With them left out, its gap fell from 0.196 (the same retrain with them left in; the original model scored 0.182) to **0.167** (95% interval 0.083–0.256). So for my model, training on those studies added about 0.03 to the gap (95% interval 0.011–0.055), but most of the gap remained. R6 and the reader, documented as never trained on them, have gaps of 0.108 and 0.145. I also looked at the reverse case. When a report mentioned something the expert said *wasn't* there, every model still ranked it well above findings that were absent from both (AUC 0.83–0.90): higher than the silent findings, though below the reported ones. In these 58 studies, the models' scores were more consistent with the report than with the expert. This data can't tell whether that's because the models learned reporting habits or because unreported findings are harder to see, since there's no independent measure of how visible each finding is. Synovitis (inflammation of the joint lining) had the most silent findings. Over half its expert-positive cases (14 of 27) weren't mentioned in the report. The Raptor-384 model and the v27 blend ranked reported synovitis at 0.96 AUC but unreported synovitis at 0.80 and 0.81; R6 went from 0.91 to 0.86. I also checked two alternative explanations. Swapping left and right knee predictions lowered lateral meniscus AUC for all eight models (v27: 0.914 to 0.874), so there was no sign of a left/right mix-up. Misranking also wasn't linked to how many MRI series a study had (Spearman correlation −0.003), so I found no sign of a problem tied to the number of series. Could better blending fix it? Not by much. Re-weighting the blend toward the expert labels narrowed the gap from 0.132 to 0.118, but that difference is within the uncertainty, and the weights were fitted on the same 58 studies. ## What this suggests Test a report-trained model against more report-derived labels and this gap can't be measured, because without a second label there are no silent findings to count. During the competition, a 200-study holdout scored with report labels favoured one blend change that the expert labels did not. On the public leaderboard that change scored 0.957 against 0.958, too small a difference to prove anything on its own. My takeaway: even a small set of image-level expert labels is useful for checking models like these, and it helps to report results separately for findings the report left out. Here, an overall AUC above 0.91 for every model didn't show the drop of 0.11–0.18 on the cases the report didn't mention. ## Limitations This is an early, exploratory finding, not a test on new scans. Only my own model's overlap with the 58 studies is verified, and only it was retrained without them. Even that retrain kept the same frozen image features and teacher model (Raptor-384), and soft labels whose weighting was tuned on the 58, so only my model's own training was held out. That R6 and the reader never trained on the 58 comes from their authors' documentation, which I couldn't check from the model files. For the Raptor models it isn't documented, and their README says the 58 were reused for model selection. My expert-weighted blends were also fitted on the 58, so their results on them are in-sample. I didn't retrain a public model: R6's recipe needs several graphics processing units (GPUs), the reader's training script isn't published, and the Raptor models used external data I don't have access to. The test set can't be used instead because it comes without reports. It's also a small study: only 58 studies and 41 silent findings, about a third of them synovitis, so the exact size of the gap is uncertain, even though its direction is consistent. The labels for whether each report mentioned a finding were made by an AI assistant under my direction, and neither a clinician nor I checked them by hand. Some of the longer reports were first read cut short, so I re-read those 19 in full; that moved 6 findings from silent to seen and slightly widened the gap. To test that, I randomly flipped up to 20% of those labels a thousand times: the gap shrank or barely changed, and stayed above zero in over 99% of runs for every model. That covers random mistakes, not systematic ones. And while the expert labels apparently come from radiologists, the organisers don't say exactly how they were made, so they aren't guaranteed to be ground truth either. These are research models built for a competition, not clinical tools, and I didn't evaluate them for clinical use. Like any model of this kind, they should only ever be used to assist a qualified expert, such as a radiologist, never to replace one. These results add one more reason for that: in these 58 studies, every model ranked findings that the report had left out lower than findings it mentioned, so a model trained on report-derived labels may be less reliable on exactly the findings reports leave out. Out of respect for the RSNA data licence, this post uses aggregate statistics only. No images, report text or per-study labels. ## Conclusions ### What the evidence supports 1. On the 58 expert-labelled studies, every model ranked expert-positive findings that the report left out lower than reported ones: a gap of 0.11–0.18 AUC, with every 95% interval excluding zero. 2. Training overlap doesn't explain the whole gap, as far as I could check. Retrained without the 58 studies, my frozen head (which still uses Raptor-384 features) kept most of its gap (0.167, 95% interval 0.083–0.256, against 0.196 with them included), and R6 and the reader, which their authors document as not trained on the 58, show gaps of 0.108 and 0.145. 3. Findings mentioned in the report but judged absent by the expert were still scored well above findings absent from both (AUC 0.83–0.90), and above the silent findings. In this sample, the models' scores align more closely with report-derived labels than with expert labels. 4. An overall AUC above 0.91 for every model does not show this drop. Measuring it needs a second, image-level reference such as expert labels; checking against report-derived labels alone cannot reveal it. 5. So even a small expert-labelled set is useful for evaluation, and I'd suggest reporting performance separately for findings the report did and did not mention. ### What it does not show 1. The mechanism. These data cannot distinguish models having learned reporting habits from unreported findings being less conspicuous. 2. Generalisation beyond this dataset and these 58 studies. The size of the effect is imprecise: the held-out interval runs from 0.083 to 0.256. 3. That the expert-label weighting caused the leaderboard improvement. The +0.001 difference is within the precision Kaggle displays. ## Read more I'm writing up the full methods and statistics separately. You can also find me on Kaggle: [codecraftedbydan](https://www.kaggle.com/codecraftedbydan). A note on tools: I used AI assistants to help write the analysis code, produce the figures and draft this post. The research question, the expert-label weighting, the decisions and the conclusions are my own. Thanks to RSNA and Kaggle for running the challenge, and to everyone who shared public notebooks. This result was built on their work.

title: Does a pretrained start help an agent keep learning? A pre-registered null, a reversal and a trade-off
excerpt: A pre-registered study of whether behaviour cloning (BC) pretraining protects a lifelong proximal policy optimisation (PPO) agent over a 40-task gridworld stream. No hypothesis was supported, a frozen random trunk beat a frozen pretrained one, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) learned late tasks best but forgot the most.
body: Silver and Sutton (2025) argue that the next generation of agents will learn mainly from their own experience, usually after starting from human data. That raises a question I wanted to test directly rather than argue about. In reinforcement learning (RL), I see the trade-off like this: demonstrations give known-good behaviour plus bias; RL gives adaptation plus reward risk. So **does a start learned from demonstrations protect the learning that follows, or limit it, when an agent has to keep learning over a long stream of tasks?** Either answer would be useful. If a pretrained start helps, that supports the "human data first, experience after" recipe. If it hurts, the recipe has a cost that someone should measure at scale. I named the project TARS, after the robot in *Interstellar*: an agent that keeps learning from what happens to it, rather than one frozen after training. The agent is trained with proximal policy optimisation (PPO) and has about one million parameters. I fixed the tests in advance, ran them on one RTX 3060 graphics processing unit (GPU), and report every result below, including the ones that went against me. **No pre-registered hypothesis was supported.** One result reversed significantly, and one variant showed a clear trade-off between learning and forgetting. The full paper, code and run data are public: [paper (Portable Document Format (PDF))](https://github.com/codecraftedbydan/behaviour-cloning-lifelong-rl/blob/main/paper.pdf), [code](https://github.com/codecraftedbydan/behaviour-cloning-lifelong-rl) and [release v0 with the run data](https://github.com/codecraftedbydan/behaviour-cloning-lifelong-rl/releases/tag/v0). ## Why primacy bias, not steady plasticity loss The first thing I tested was whether my task stream causes a steady loss of plasticity at all: the slow decline in an agent's ability to learn new tasks that Dohare et al. (2024) documented. If there is nothing to lose, there is nothing for pretraining to protect. There wasn't, at this scale. In a 40-task pilot, the pre-registered slope of relative adaptation over tasks was −0.0044, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of [−0.0073, +0.0018]. In the 200-task follow-up I had committed to in advance, it was +0.00009 [−0.00048, +0.00052] per task. Both intervals include 0. What the pilots did show was a collapse at the first task switch, a pattern known as primacy bias (Nikishin et al., 2022). Relative adaptation on task 2 minus task 1 was −0.72 [−0.97, −0.26] in the 40-task pilot. A probe that gave a frozen copy of the stream agent's trunk fresh heads recovered most of the gap: its relative adaptation was −0.10, against −0.72 for the stream agent on the same tasks, a paired difference of +0.59 [+0.46, +0.70]. That points at the heads, optimiser state and normalisation statistics rather than the shared features. The switch to testing primacy bias was not a pivot after seeing the pilots. I wrote the fallback down before either run: if both slopes came back null, the main study would ask whether pretraining softens the collapse at the first switch instead. ## Setup **Environment.** Each task is a fully observed 8×8 gridworld. Each new task changes exactly one thing about the previous one: the goal moves, the action mapping is permuted, or the observation layout is permuted. After every third new task, an earlier task is revisited, giving 40 new tasks and 53 blocks per stream. The agent is never told which task it is on or when a switch happens. **Pretraining.** Behaviour cloning (BC): supervised copying of a shortest-path planner's actions on tasks disjoint from every test stream. The planner takes a random action 15% of the time and then recovers, so the demonstrations include recovering from mistakes. **Cells.** Ten cells, each on the same 25 seeds: - scratch and pretrained, both with full fine-tuning; - three other ways of updating a pretrained network: low-rank adaptation (LoRA), a frozen pretrained trunk with only the heads trained, and kickstarting (a penalty pulling the agent towards the cloned policy early on); - a frozen *random* trunk, as a control for the frozen pretrained one; - PPO with layer normalisation (LN), scratch and pretrained, against the parallelised Q-network (PQN), scratch and pretrained, to compare value-based and policy-gradient learning with layer normalisation held fixed. ## The measure, and why it depends on the fresh agent Every task in the stream is also learned by a *fresh* agent: the same architecture and budget, from a random initialisation. That keeps task difficulty out of the measure, since later tasks may simply be harder. The agent gets a reward of 1 − 0.9t/64 for reaching the goal at step t, and I divide returns by the shortest-path optimum for that task, so 1 is optimal. Adaptation on a task is the area under the curve (AUC) of normalised training return over the task's 100 updates. **Relative adaptation** is the stream agent's AUC minus the fresh agent's AUC on the same task. Zero means the stream agent learns the task as fast as a fresh agent would. Negative means it has become a worse learner. The primary test, D, compares late learning, on new tasks 21–40: the interquartile mean (IQM) of relative adaptation for the pretrained agent minus the same for the scratch agent. The IQM is the mean of the middle 50% of values, taken over all seeds × tasks, following Agarwal et al. (2021). The interval comes from a paired, stratified bootstrap: within each task, seeds are resampled, and the same draw is used for both cells because they share fresh agents. To count, D had to be at least 0.093 with an interval excluding 0. That gap is 10% of the fresh agent's late AUC of 0.934. **A subtraction can be gamed by weakening the baseline.** My learning-rate sweep showed this happening. Under full fine-tuning from pretraining, the stream agent's raw late AUC peaked at a learning rate of 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ (0.257) and fell to 0.168 at 10⁻³. But the fresh agent, trained at the same rate, fell further, from 0.912 to 0.602, so relative adaptation still favoured 10⁻³. The original selection rule would have picked the learning rate that made the *baseline* worse. So I changed the rule: pick each cell's learning rate by raw stream AUC, and tune each fresh baseline separately, as Patterson et al. (2024) recommend. I made that change after the sweep and before any counted run, dated it with its reason, and report the original rule's picks as a sensitivity result. It's the change in this study I'd most want a reviewer to scrutinise, which is why the paper reports raw AUC beside the relative measure for every result. ## Results No pre-registered hypothesis was supported. **Primary test.** The pretraining effect on late relative adaptation was D = +0.045, with a 95% CI of [+0.000, +0.088]. The lower bound sits at 0 within bootstrap noise: across bootstrap random seeds it moves by about ±0.002, so I don't read the interval as excluding 0. The verdict doesn't rest on the interval anyway. D is about half the 0.093 gap, so any benefit was *not detected at this resolution*. That is not the same as "no effect"; it means any real benefit is smaller than this study can resolve. Every sensitivity version agrees, and none meets the gap. **Primacy bias.** The secondary test, pretrained minus scratch on the size of the collapse from task 1 to task 2, gave +0.200 [−0.103, +0.449]. The point estimate clears the gap, but the interval includes 0. It also leans on five seeds whose task 2 still shared the observation layout and action mapping used in pretraining. Without them, it shrinks to +0.034 [−0.276, +0.332]. The H labels are the hypotheses I pre-registered. For forgetting, a higher number means more forgetting. - **H1′ (primary)**, late relative adaptation, pretrained − scratch: +0.045 [+0.000, +0.088]. Not supported; not detected at this resolution. - **H1′-b**, primacy bias, pretrained − scratch: +0.200 [−0.103, +0.449]. Not supported. - **H3**, forgetting, LoRA − full fine-tuning: +0.453 [+0.343, +0.558]. Not supported; LoRA forgets *more*. - **H5**, pretraining effect, PPO with LN − PQN: +0.018 [−0.013, +0.052]. Not supported. - **H6**, late relative adaptation, frozen pretrained − frozen random: −0.109 [−0.149, −0.073]. Not supported; a significant reversal. The paper has the full table for all ten cells, aggregated two ways; the ordering of cells I rely on is the same either way. The PQN cells look good on relative adaptation only because PQN's own fresh agent is weak, so their raw AUC is the number to read. ## The reversal: a frozen random trunk beat a frozen pretrained one Hypothesis H6 said that, with only the heads trained, a frozen *pretrained* trunk would support late learning better than a frozen *random* one. The opposite happened: frozen pretrained minus frozen random was −0.109 [−0.149, −0.073]. The interval excludes 0 and the difference is bigger than the gap, so it is a significant reversal. The raw numbers make it vivid. Per seed, the frozen random trunk reached a raw late AUC of 0.213, close to full fine-tuning's 0.215. The frozen pretrained trunk reached 0.032. The caveat matters: both frozen cells picked a learning rate of 10⁻⁴, the bottom edge of the grid, so both sets of heads may be under-trained. That could change the size of the gap, though it would not obviously reverse it. ## The LoRA trade-off Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) trains a small low-rank update on top of frozen pretrained weights. It had the best late learning of any PPO cell: a per-seed late relative adaptation of −0.481, against −0.692 for full fine-tuning, and a late end-of-block score of 0.514, the highest of any cell. It also forgot the most. Backward transfer (BWT), the score on a task at a later point minus the score right after it was last trained, was −0.479 over all revisits. Against full fine-tuning, LoRA's forgetting was +0.453 [+0.343, +0.558] worse. That runs against the "learns less and forgets less" result reported for LoRA in large language models (Biderman et al., 2024), though I offer that only as a post-hoc contrast. The figure shows the trade-off seed by seed: seeds that learned more late in the stream tended to lose more. *Per-seed LoRA late end-of-block score against backward transfer. Left: revisits in the late window, 23 seeds (two seeds have no revisit there). Right: end of stream, all 25 seeds.* There is a confound I can't remove after the fact. LoRA ran at a learning rate of 10⁻³ against 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ for full fine-tuning, so its better learning and its extra forgetting can't be put down to the low-rank update alone. Kickstarting barely registered. Its penalty, a Kullback–Leibler (KL) term pulling the agent towards the cloned policy, was a brief early nudge: it was active in at most 2 of 53 blocks, and it did not help. Its chosen coefficient, 0.01, was also at the edge of its grid. ## What I take from it In this setting, the hand-off from demonstrations to experience was neither the protection nor the obstacle I set out to look for. Under full fine-tuning, the behaviour-cloned start did not carry the agent past the collapse at the first switch, and it did not detectably make later learning worse either. As frozen features it was worse than random ones. In descriptive comparisons, the update method moved late learning more than the starting point did. That comes with learning-rate confounds, so I treat it as a pointer for the next study rather than a finding. What happens during the experience phase seems to matter more than where the agent starts. That is a statement about one small gridworld family and one network size. It is not evidence about foundation-model scale. ## What went wrong **Behaviour cloning memorised the scrambles.** In my first design, every task, including the demonstration tasks, had its own random observation and action permutation. Cloning fitted the training tasks but stayed at chance on held-out ones (accuracy 0.20–0.29), and early stopping picked epoch 0. The "pretrained" agent was bit-identical to scratch. I caught this on development seeds and fixed it, before any official run, by giving the demonstrations and task 1 a shared layout. **Two development gates failed.** Before the main runs, I required pretraining to beat scratch on task 1. It didn't: the paired IQM was about −0.13, so pretraining made task 1 *worse*. A second gate, on the pretrained critic's value loss, failed on one seed. My rules didn't say what happens after a failed gate, so I had to rule on it afterwards: keep the design, record both failures with their diagnostics, and report task 1 as negative transfer. **Non-determinism.** GPU runs at full 32-bit precision weren't bitwise reproducible, and on the central processing unit (CPU) a seed's result depended on which seeds shared its batch: one PQN seed reached optimal return alone and 0.0 in a three-seed batch. **What I didn't run.** The network-size comparison (H4) was dropped for compute budget before any run, so I make no claim about scale. The reset arms (H7) weren't run either. And in the baseline check against PureJaxRL, I set a rule that PureJaxRL passes against itself only 33% of the time. That was my error. ## Lessons - **Write the fallback before the pilot.** The pivot to primacy bias was defensible only because it was on paper first. - **Say in advance what follows a failed gate.** I didn't, and I had to rule on it after the fact. - **Never trust a relative measure without its raw parts beside it.** A subtraction can improve because the baseline got worse. - **With artificial intelligence (AI) assistance, the bottleneck moves to checking.** The code and analysis here were built with AI help. Every analysis that counts towards a result was re-run independently and reproduced its results file byte for byte before I accepted it. I designed the study and made every ruling myself, and I think that split is the right one. ## Read more - [Paper (PDF)](https://github.com/codecraftedbydan/behaviour-cloning-lifelong-rl/blob/main/paper.pdf), with the full methods, every cell and the pre-registration. - [Code and results](https://github.com/codecraftedbydan/behaviour-cloning-lifelong-rl), MIT licence. `REPRODUCE.md` recomputes every number in the paper from the released data in about a minute on a CPU. - [Release v0](https://github.com/codecraftedbydan/behaviour-cloning-lifelong-rl/releases/tag/v0), with the run data and checksums. - Related: Silver and Sutton (2025), *Welcome to the Era of Experience*; Nikishin et al. (2022) on primacy bias; Dohare et al. (2024) on loss of plasticity; Wołczyk et al. (2024) on forgetting in fine-tuned RL agents.
